# Sensitive Multiplexed MicroRNA Spatial Profiling and Data Classification Framework Applied to Murine Breast Tumors

**Authors:** Omar N. Mohd; Yujing J. Heng; Lin Wang; Abhishek Thavamani; Erica S. Massicott; Gerburg M. Wulf; Frank J. Slack; Patrick S. Doyle

**Affiliations:** †Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139, United States | §Departments of Pathology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts 02215, United States | ‖Departments of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts 02215, United States | ¶Harvard Medical School Initiative for RNA Medicine, Departments of Pathology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts 02215, United States | ‡Department of Chemical Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139, United States

## Abstract

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small RNAs that are often dysregulated in many diseases, including cancers. They are highly tissue specific and stable, thus making them particularly useful as biomarkers. As the spatial transcriptomics field advances, protocols that enable highly sensitive and spatially resolved detection become necessary to maximize the information gained from samples. This is especially true of miRNAs where the location of where they are expressed within tissue can provide prognostic value with regards to patient outcome. Equally as important as detection are ways to assess and visualize the miRNA’s spatial information in order to leverage the power of spatial transcriptomics over that of traditional non-spatial bulk assays. We present a highly sensitive methodology that simultaneously quantitates and spatially detects seven miRNAs in situ on formalin-fixed paraffin embedded tissue sections. This method utilizes rolling circle amplification (RCA) in conjunction with a dual scanning approach in nanoliter well arrays with embedded hydrogel posts. The hydrogel posts are functionalized with DNA-probes that enable the detection of miRNAs across a large dynamic range (four orders of magnitude) and a limit of detection of 0.17 zeptomoles (1.7×10−4 attomoles). We applied our methodology coupled with a data analysis pipeline to K14-Cre Brca1f/fTp53f/f murine breast tumors to showcase the information gained from this approach.

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small (20–23 base pairs) non-protein coding RNAs with various regulatory functions for many biological processes. They can be dysregulated in diseases, including cancers.1–4 Many miRNAs serve as tumor suppressors while others are abundant in tumors due to dysregulation.5–9 In various cancers, the abundance of miRNAs as well as their location within the tissue architecture have been shown to have a direct correlation with the patient outcome.9–14

There is increasing interest in utilizing miRNAs as disease biomarkers due to their abundance, stability and tissue specificity.15–18 We previously designed a device that consists of a nanoliter well array with hydrogel posts in each well containing miRNA detecting DNA probes (Figure 1A).19,20 Our technology can quantitatively measure multiple miRNAs while maintaining their spatial information within the tissue.

As with other spatial transcriptomics technologies, having the capability to detect small amounts of the biomarker of interest is important given the nature of the sample and abundance of the biomarker. While other technologies such as real time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) along with microdissection of a sample have been able to achieve semi-quantitative amplification along with preserving the spatial information, the very nature of RT-qPCR introduces a quantification bias, due to the fact that the biomarker itself is being amplified.21 In another of our prior works,22,23 we utilized an amplification protocol for the detection of miRNAs non-spatially using rolling circle amplification (RCA). RCA is an isothermal amplification scheme.24–27 Unlike RT-qPCR, we utilized RCA to amplify the detection element rather than the biomarker and RCA can be readily incorporated into our existing nanoliter well array.28,29

In recent years, there have been both technological and analytical techniques devised to address the spatial detection of other biomarkers such as messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and cell protein markers.30,31 MiRNA detection, however, remains a relatively unexplored area of research. In order to leverage the power of spatial transcriptomics over traditional bulk assays, various analysis and visualization techniques have been adopted from other fields, namely geographic sciences, and natural language processing for their focus on spatial heterogeneity visualization and feature detection respectively.32–34 These include the use of spatial Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) as a means of feature discovery both spatially within the samples it is applied to, and with regards to the data that the LDA model is trained on.31–33,35,36 This can further be simplified using commonly used linear dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA along with a clustering algorithm such as k-Means for utilizing spatial miRNA data for classification purposes.35,37,38

In this paper, we report an optimized protocol for the quantitative, multiplexed, and spatial detection of miRNAs in formalin fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) tissue sections, as well as a novel analysis pipeline for assessing spatially resolved miRNA data. We implement an RCA scheme, and employ a novel approach to improve the limit of detection (LOD) of our device while also maintaining quantitative detection of miRNAs of high abundance that would normally be amplified to the point of sensor saturation, thus effectively expanding the overall dynamic range of our device. We then showcase how combining miRNA expression and spatial information can classify murine breast tumors as drug sensitive or resistant by training data acquired using our new RCA protocol on an LDA model and further analyzed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with k-means clustering.

## EXPERIMENTAL SECTION

### Device Fabrication.

Nanoliter well arrays were fabricated with hydrogel posts containing miRNA complimentary DNA probes as previously described19,20 with further optimizations. The nanoliter wells were fabricated by first activating a glass coverslip surface (Electron Microscopy Sciences) in a 1M NaOH bath, followed by silanization using 3-(Trimethoxysilyl)propyl methacrylate (Millipore Sigma). A pattered polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS, Electron Microscopy Sciences) mold was placed on the silanized glass surface, filled with the optical adhesive NOA-81 (Thorlabs), and then polymerized via exposure to a UV lamp. The resulting polymerized NOA-81 and salinized glass surface constitutes the nanoliter well array. The hydrogels embedded within each well of the array were fabricated as previously published.19,20 A prepolymer solution containing the desired DNA probes (Table S1) is created. This prepolymer solution consists of 36% (v/v) poly(ethylene glycol) 200 g/mol, 18% (v/v) poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate 700 g/mol, 4.5% (v/v) Darocur 1173 photoinitiator (2-hydroxy-2-methylpropiophenone), and 41.5% (v/v) ~1X Tris EDTA buffer (1XTE), and DNA probes. The prepolymer solution is used to fill the wells with a PDMS block sealing the top of the arrays. A chrome mask (Photo Sciences) with the desired hydrogel post cross-sectional dimensions is then aligned to the array and a UV light source39 (Thor Labs) is applied through the mask and onto the wells to polymerize the prepolymer in each well, thus resulting in a hydrogel that is functionalized with the desired probes. A brightfield image of the resulting wells and posts is presented in Figure 1B.

### Hybridization and Ligation Protocol.

A hybridization solution is created consisting of 350 mM NaCl in 1X Tris-EDTA buffer with 0.05% Tween 20 (1X TET), 2% (w/v) sodium dodecyl sulfate (Sigma Aldrich), and 32 U/mL of proteinase K (New England Biolabs).19,20 Thirty microliters of this hybridization solution is placed on top of the well array and spread around the array for 10 seconds to ensure homogeneity within the wells. The well array is then sealed with a FFPE tissue section, such that hybridization buffer is sandwiched in between the array and the tissue sample. To ensure a tight seal, we placed magnets (Grainger) on the top and bottom of the seal. To initiate both hybridization and freeing the miRNAs from our sample, we placed the sealed array inside a 55°C oven for 3 hours to allow for adequate hybridization of our miRNAs. The presence of proteinase K and a subsequent 10 minute 80°C enzyme deactivation step ensure that any possible RNases are denatured. After the hybridization step, the tissue section and magnets are removed and the well array is washed using our wash buffer (50 mM NaCL 1X TET). A ligation solution is introduced to ligate a linker sequence (Table S1) that is necessary to perform RCA amplification. The ligation solution consists of 10% (w/w) 1X NEBuffer 2 (New England Biolabs), 2.5% (w/w) 250 μM ATP (New England Biolabs), 86.9% (w/w) 1X TET, 0.2% (w/w) 800 U/mL T4 DNA ligase (New England Biolabs), and 0.4% (w/w) RCA linker 40 nM. The ligation solution is applied to the array at room temperature for 1 hour.

### RCA Assay Protocol.

The RCA protocol follows from the ligation step described previously20 and in Figure 1C. The protocol consists of three major steps, taken between ligation and fluorescent labeling, these are: (1) circle annealing, (2) RCA, and (3) reporter labeling. As can be seen in Figure 1C, in the circle annealing step, a 250 μL solution of our wash buffer along with lab synthesized circular DNA templates (at a concentration of 150 nM) are introduced to the array using a spacer (Figure S2). The annealing reaction takes place at 45°C in a Vortemp 56 incubator (Labnet) for one hour. During this step, precautions are taken to ensure no drying takes place. This is done by introducing a 3.5 mm diameter petri dish (Falcon) that contains deionized water inside the incubator as well as using a parafilm sealant on the lid of the spacer to prevent any drying from within the spacer-array region where the circles-containing wash buffer is placed.

After the circle annealing step, the buffer is aspirated and the array-spacer region is washed with 250 μL of wash buffer four times (for a total of 1 mL of wash buffer). The RCA step occurs after washing, in which a specially made solution of reagents and the enzyme Phi-29 DNA Polymerase is introduced to begin the RCA process.22 The solution is 250 μL and consists of : (1) 25 μL of NEB2 (New England Biolabs Buffer 2, New England Biolabs) at a 10 X concentration, (2) 207.5 μL of 1XTET, (3) 2.5 μL BSA (Bovine Serum Albumin) at a concentration of 20 mg/mL, (4) 1.25 μL of DTT (Dithioerythritol, Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 1M concentration, (5) 3.75 μL of dNTPs (Deoxy Nucleoside Triphosphates, New England Biolabs) at a concentration of 10 mM, and lastly (6) 10 μL of phi29 DNA Polymerase (New England Biolabs) at a concentration of 10,000 U/mL. This solution is introduced to the array via spacer and placed in the Vortemp incubator with the same exact precautions taken to prevent drying as was done in the circle annealing step. The RCA step is carried out for 4 hours at a temperature of 30°C in the incubator. After this step is complete, the solution in-between the spacer is aspirated and the array is washed with 1 mL of wash buffer as was done in the circle annealing step.

The final step consists of adding in reporter sequences (Table S1) functionalized with biotin so that fluorescent labeling can be carried out using the fluorophore SAPE (Streptavidin-Phycoerythrin, Thermo Fisher Scientific). The reporter solution is 250 μL and consists of: (1) 1.25 μL of a combination of 2 different biotinylated reporter sequences that are complimentary to the RCA product (Integrated DNA Technologies) each at a concentration of 10 μM, and (2) 248.75 μL of the wash buffer. This step is carried for 1 hour at room temperature (25°C) using the same precautions to prevent drying as the two previous steps with exception of using the Parafilm. After this step the solution in between the spacer is aspirated and another round of 1 mL wash buffer is applied. After these three steps, the SAPE labeling step follows previous works19,20 and consists of applying a 250 μL solution to the array that consists of 2.5 μL of SAPE solution at a concentration of 1mg/mL, and 247.5 μL wash buffer. This solution is applied for one hour at room temperature (25°C) away from light, and is then aspirated with 1 mL of wash buffer as was previously done, and taken to a slide scanner for imaging. Assay times range from 6–12 hours depending on the amount of amplification needed. In comparison, other miRNA detection techniques, namely ones based in situ hybridization, PCR, or sequencing techniques, have assay times of ~24–48 hours, ~16 hours, and ~ a couple of days respectively.

### Data Acquisition and Analysis.

Both data acquisition and analysis procedures have significantly changed from previous works to accommodate the application of RCA and maximize information output. Data analysis consists of using a slide scanner at a resolution of 5μm per pixel (GenePix 4400A, Molecular Devices) to obtain a fluorescent read out of our arrays as seen in Figure 1D. To accommodate the application of the RCA protocol which amplifies the fluorescent signal of the array, extra steps needed to be taken to ensure no data loss occurs during the scanning step. While in previous work19,20 arrays were scanned at a single scanner gain, the fact that the signal has been amplified during RCA means that it can result in signal amplification to a point that would result in saturation, as the scanner is limited to a 16-bit output. To circumnavigate this issue, the scanner gain was characterized as shown in Figure 3B, in order to find out at what lower gain can the effect of the amplification be offset such that the higher signals would not saturate. This, however, would mean that in order to attain a signal that fully takes advantage of the RCA amplification (to measure lower signals), but also the information of higher signals, we would need to scan twice. Once at a higher gain (gain of 500) to reap the benefits of amplification, and once at a lower gain (gain of 200) to attain the signals that would saturate otherwise. Photobleaching as a result of multiple scans is minimal with only an average signal loss of 2% after two scans as shown in Figure 3A. Since each array results in two fluorescent images taken at two different gains, data analysis was changed in order to create a single output form these two inputs. This was done efficiently by using a nonlinear classifier to categorize each post signal as either derivable from the 500-gain scan or the 200-gain scan. Using a threshold value, any data that was near saturation in the 500-gain data was extracted from the 200-gain data and then properly scaled such that a single data output is constructed and miRNA amount value can be calculated using calibration curves.

### Murine breast tumors.

The K14-Cre Brca1f/fTp53f/f transgenic mouse model develops breast tumors driven by the loss of Brca1 induced by tissue-specific knock-out via the K14-activated Cre-recombinase. Tumor fragments from an original tumor never treated with olaparib, a FDA-approved Poly(ADP-ribose) Polymerase (PARP)-inhibitor indicative for BRCA1/2mut tumors, were implanted into recipient FVB/NJ mice (n=4). These tumors remain sensitive to olaparib. Another set of mice were implanted with fragments from a different tumor that was previously treated long-term with olaparib and had gained resistance (n=4).

Tumors were left to develop and were untreated for this study. Recipient mice were euthanized within 20 days when the tumors reached 20 mm. Tumors were harvested, fixed in formalin for 48 hours, and stored in 70% ethanol at 4°C. A portion of each tumor then underwent standard histology processing into FFPE tissue blocks and 5 μm tissue sections were obtained for hematoxylin and eosin (H&E staining) and for the multiplex miRNA assay. The assays were conducted in batches of three, run simultaneously, on the tissue sections adjacent to the ones used for H&E staining. We specifically constructed our miRNA panel such that each miRNA is related to the development and progress of BRCA tumors.40–43 All animal experiments were conducted in accordance with Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee-approved protocols at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (052–2020-23).

### Spatial LDA model training and classification.

Applying the calibration curve shown in Figure 3D as well as the other calibration curves for the remainder of the panel (Figure S1) to various tissue samples results in spatial miRNA data, as shown in Figure 5A. A spatial LDA model was trained on this data to determine which combinations of miRNAs, in the form of topics, can be used for feature discovery within the spatial miRNA data as well as for classifying the tissue samples. The spatial LDA model was trained on 43,904 miRNA data points from across 8 distinct tissue samples. This was done in MATLAB (Scripts S1–S4) by systemically creating a data table, where the columns represent the seven miRNAs in our panel and each row represents a single well within one sample for a total of 784 wells per sample (6,272 wells for all samples combined). Hyper parameter tuning was necessary in order to determine the appropriate number of topics for the model to solve for. The most effective topic number for taking into account a sufficient number of the miRNAs of our panel, was a total of 4 topics. In addition, we needed to determine which solver would be appropriate for our application case. Given that we are not running thousands of samples, we opted for the most accurate solver for the LDA model and used Collapsed Gibbs Sampling (CBS)44 which calculates the miRNA weighting probabilities for our topics in small batches (we chose 500 samples, or about ~50 wells per batch to calculate the weighting in each iteration of the training).

After training the model, the learned miRNA weights for each topic (Figure 5B) were then applied on a well-by-well basis for every well in our samples, whereby the weighting of the miRNAs for each topic is used to calculate a value for each topic in each well, and the topic with the highest value is then associated with that well. As displayed in Figure 5C. We can also simplify the spatial LDA results of Figure 5C into the percentage of the tissue that has been assigned to each topic for colorimetric classification, as shown in Figure 5D. To automate classification and quantify it, we applied PCA to the topic percentages from Figure 5D and to average miRNA values (in attomoles) in the tissue samples for comparison with the LDA output. We finally used k-means clustering45 with random initialization to cluster the PCA data into two categories as shown in Figure 5E. The resulting clusters are then assessed both intrinsically and extrinsically for both the LDA output and the average miRNA output. The intrinsic method used was calculating the adjusted rand index (ARI)46,47 to compare the predicted cluster values and the ground truth. An ARI of one indicates that the predicted clusters and the ground truth are exactly the same, and an ARI of zero indicates that predicted clusters are seemingly random when compared to the ground truth, with any negative ARI value indicating that the predictions are less accurate than what would be expected from a random classification.46–48 The extrinsic method used was the silhouette coefficient (SC)45,49 which assesses the quality of clusters rather than the accuracy, whereby the further apart each unique cluster is and smaller its spread, the higher the silhouette coefficient would be. A silhouette coefficient of zero indicates that the separation between the clusters is so small to the point where they are indistinguishable, and a score of one indicates that the clusters are separate and far apart.45,49

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

### Characterizing RCA Efficacy.

RCA efficacy was characterized by examining the various components of the RCA protocol as well as the efficiency of the isothermal amplification. In order for RCA occur, a circular single stranded DNA template needs to be synthesized by ligating the two ends of a linear single stranded DNA template (see Table S5). The output of the circle synthesis was characterized in two steps. The first ensuring that the end product is a single stranded DNA sequence, which was characterized by a NanoDrop (Thermo Fisher Scientific). For pure nucleic acids, taking the ratio of the absorbance at 260 nm and 280 nm (A260/A280) results in a number greater than 1.8. As noted in (Table S3), the resulting ratio for our circle sample is greater than 2 and can thus be considered a pure nucleic acid sample. In the second step, gel electrophoresis was used to confirm that the linear 50 base pair DNA is converted into a circle. Figure 2B shows that the linear DNA template precursor aligns with the 50 base band of a low molecular weight ladder (Integrated DNA Technologies) and that the circular DNA runs slower in the gel, as expected.

As noted in Figure 1C, during the RCA step, the sequence of the annealed circle template is continuously duplicated for the entire 4-hour RCA step, this results in a long DNA strand attached to the linker sequence of each bound probe. Thus, once the strand is fluorescently labeled, a characteristic “speckling” effect can be visually ascertained as seen in Figure 2A. and as has been noted in previous works.22,23 In addition to visual confirmation, the amplification rate of RCA was quantitatively measured by varying the duration of the RCA step (Figure 2C) which, as noted previously22,23, is a linear amplification process that results in nearly a 100-fold amplification in 4 hours.

### Validating RCA Protocol.

The RCA protocol was validated by ensuring the soundness of the methods used to extract data from the amplified assay signal and by comparison to non-amplified assays. As can be seen in Figure 3C at a standard scanner gain of 500, lower miRNA amounts which were immeasurable in prior work20 can be detected with relatively high fluorescent signal (measured in AFUs, arbitrary florescent units). Yet at the same scanner gain for higher miRNA amounts which were previously measurable, we see the signal plateauing at the 16-bit scanner limit. To overcome this scanner limitation, more than one scan was performed for each array. A scan at a gain of 500 was used to measure lower amounts of miRNA and a scan at a gain of 200 was used to measure higher amounts miRNA. Since the SAPE fluorophore, like many others, is prone to photobleaching after excitation, it was necessary to examine the effect of multiple scans on SAPE signal. As shown in Figure 3A, applying subsequent scans to an array does have a reduction in signal, yet at the second scan mark, which is what is applied in this method, the average signal reduction is only 2% and at the miRNA amounts of interest (noted in Figure 3C) a 2% loss in signal is well below the CV (coefficient of variation) that is expected from our protocol (noted by the error bars in Figure 3C).

In addition to addressing concerns of photobleaching, it was necessary to determine the appropriate gains at which to scan the array. As noted in Figure 3B, an array’s average signal was calculated at various scanner gains to determine the relationship between scanner gain and AFU. The choice of a gain of 500 is twofold: it is the gain at which the arrays were scanned at in previous work20, and it is the gain at which the amplified signal of the lower miRNA amounts neither saturate near the upper end, nor is too low on the lower end. The choice of a gain of 200 was determined by fitting the points in Figure 3B to a logarithmic function and analytically calculating the gain at which the output signal is nearly 100-fold less than that of a gain of 500.

In Figure 4A and Figure 4B the RCA protocol was applied and the resulting heat maps from the two scans are shown. In Figure 4A we show the result of RCA in the non-saturated (not white) center of the heatmap. Since the miRNA being examined happens to be highly abundant, many of the wells are saturated. To garner the full benefit of the amplification, we scanned the data at a lower gain of 200 so we can analyze the data in wells that would be saturated at a higher gain. A composite scan (Figure 4C) was then created that is neither saturated at higher miRNA amounts as is in the 500-gain scan, and preserves the lower amount miRNA data that is lost in the 200-gain scan. After validating the methods used for data acquisition, these new methods were applied to female K14-Cre BRCA1f/fTp53f/f murine breast tumors. We constructed a composite calibration curve (Figure 3D) by scaling the 200-gain data, seen in Figure 3C, to the 500-gain curve, by using a scaling factor. The scaling factor was calculated by first choosing a miRNA amount that is detectable at both the 500-gain and the 200-gain, and then by taking the ratio of the signal at both gains. For our experiments we found the signal at 0.03 attomoles to be detectible across both gains for all the miRNAs in our panel, thus, the scaling factor was constructed using that miRNA amount. In addition to creating a composite calibration curve, the signals in the 500-gain array data (Figure 4A) that reached saturation point, were recalculated using the 200-gain data via a nonlinear classifier, to make the process more efficient. The result of using both the scaled-up calibration curve and the classifier is the composite heatmap shown in Figure 4C. While the composite heatmap retains the miRNA data for both high and low amounts, the necessity of using the RCA protocol has to be established.

While miRNA quantities above 0.03 attomoles can be measured using the non-RCA protocol described in our previous work20, the need for the RCA protocol is dependent on samples and miRNA panel. In the tissue samples shown in Figures 4 and 5, multiple clinically relevant miRNAs were found in amounts much lower than the limit of detection of the non-RCA protocol. The LOD is defined as the miRNA amount that corresponds to a signal three times the standard deviation of the signal when there is no miRNA target is present. As can be seen in the miR-16 RCA heatmap in Figure 4D, in the central area of the heatmap there is a relatively lower signal than the peripheral tissue. Quantitatively examining the data while making note of the LOD, it can be seen that there are data points that would fall below the non-RCA LOD but that fall within the detection window of the RCA protocol. This demonstrates the utility of the RCA protocol.

### Spatial LDA Analysis, classification, and interpretation.

Reconstructed, high dynamic range spatial miRNA data was gathered by applying the RCA protocol and novel scanning approach to eight murine breast tumor FFPE sections.50–52

While our new RCA protocol allows us to quantify miRNA values below the LOD of the standard protocol (Figure 4D), we are left with a massive data set in both quantity and dimension. For the eight tissue samples we assessed, we have 43,904 data values along with their spatial information; methods to both analyze this data as well as visualize it are necessary. While we know a priori whether the tumor was sensitive (S) or resistant (R) to olaparib, we did not use this information in our analysis. We labelled the samples a to h in a randomized blind manner. We then examined how classification, utilizing the spatial miRNA data, compared to the ground truth. In addition to categorizing our samples, we also wanted to learn about the miRNAs that would help with such categorization, and to leverage the spatial aspect of our miRNA data as opposed to bulk analysis of the miRNAs across the samples. Due to the nature of our data, and the relatively small number of samples we were examining, we ruled out the use of a supervised learning approach to classification, as well as the lack of output that such an approach would generate with regards to understanding why a classification is given as opposed to simply assessing how accurate the classification is. As such we utilized an unsupervised learning technique commonly utilized in natural language processing, known as LDA.32,33 With respect to our use case, LDA could be applied spatially to examine miRNA counts in our panel, and in return, it can provide both information about which weighted combinations of miRNA values (known as topics) can be used to best categorize our samples spatially, thus allowing us to classify our samples while also preserving meaning behind such classification.

As can be seen in Figure 5A, we trained our LDA model using data input from the heat maps of our spatial miRNA data. This allowed us to learn four topics, and the respective miRNA weights that comprise these topics (Figure 5B). The two most important topics with regards to classification are topics one and two which, in both Figure 5C and 5D, can be seen to correlate with whether a sample is resistant or sensitive to olaparib. Since we know the weighting of each miRNA for each of these topics, we can thus interpret that let-7a is an important miRNA in olaparib resistance tumors while miR-21 is involved in conferring olaparib sensitivity. Let-7a is a tumor suppressor.41 miR-21 is oncogenic and promotes tumor invasion into healthy stromal tissue.17 Topics 3 and 4 are primarily informed by miR34a/miR200c, and miR-19a/miR30c respectively. Mir34a is associated with cancer aggressiveness while miR200c is associated with cancer metastasis.53,54 Mir19a is a known oncogene while miR30c is a tumor inhibitor.55,56 LDA topics do not provide indication of direction of change. In-depth understanding of the seven miRNAs of interest will be elucidated in a follow up publication.

We can easily classify our samples colorimetrically (Figure 5D) based off of how much of the tissue is associated with each topic. We can also do this spatially, as in Figure 5C, and see how the topics are associated spatially to each part of the tissue. Furthermore, we can quantify our classification approach for a more systematic application to newer samples, as well as to highlight the power that can be leveraged from spatial miRNA data as opposed to non-spatial, or averaged miRNA values for the samples. To do this, we performed PCA on both the LDA output for each sample and for the spatially averaged miRNA values (mimicking a bulk assay) for each sample (Table S4). After PCA, we then applied an unsupervised clustering algorithm, k-means, to be performed 100 times for each PCA data set in Figure 5E. We then used various statistical approaches to assess the significance of the data clusters in both classification accuracy, and quality of clustering in Figure 5F.

What can be confirmed visually when comparing Figure 5E.i and Figure 5E.ii is also attested to in Figure 5F. We clearly saw two distinct and well separated clusters in Figure 5E.i for our LDA output while a much more convoluted clustering took place for the averaged miRNA data. In terms of accuracy, the randomly initialized k-means algorithm correctly clustered the LDA output in all of the 100 trials. The averaged miRNA output had much more unpredictable cluster assignments, which we quantified using the ARI in Figure 5F.ii, a commonly used metric for data clustering. The ARI for the averaged miRNA data was nearly 0.2, which indicates the cluster assignments being close to random. We also assessed the quality of the clustering for both data types using the SC. Whereas the mean SC score is close to one for the LDA output, indicating well separated clusters, the mean SC for the averaged miRNA data was ~0.44, indicating weak separation of the clusters. Thus, in terms of both accuracy and quality of clusters the LDA of the spatial miRNA data is superior to that over the non-spatial average miRNA values.

## CONCLUSIONS

We developed and applied an RCA protocol and a novel data acquisition method to improve the LOD of multiplexed spatial miRNA detection down to a value of 0.17 zeptomoles as well as improve the overall dynamic range of our assay. The utility of this new approach has been demonstrated on clinically relevant murine samples. Clinically relevant low abundant miRNA data, that was previously undetectable, can now be quantified using our new method due to our improved LOD. The multiplexed spatial miRNA data output of this new method was also shown to be useful for classifying drug resistance in samples a priori. We have shown that reliably assessing drug resistance in bulk miRNA assays was not possible, while we could concretely classify drug resistance in samples by utilizing spatial miRNA data.
